p.b: This compilation only includes editorial change

preface.p: This is a compilation of the Radiocommunications Legislation Amendment (Reform and Modernisation) Act 2020 that shows the text of the law as amended and in force on 15 September 2021 (the compilation date).
The notes at the end of this compilation (the endnotes) include information about amending laws and the amendment history of provisions of the compiled law.

The effect of uncommenced amendments is not shown in the text of the compiled law. Any uncommenced amendments affecting the law are accessible on the Legislation Register (www.legislation.gov.au). The details of amendments made up to, but not commenced at, the compilation date are underlined in the endnotes. For more information on any uncommenced amendments, see the series page on the Legislation Register for the compiled law.

p.b: Application, saving and transitional provisions for provisions and amendments

preface.p: If the operation of a provision or amendment of the compiled law is affected by an application, saving or transitional provision that is not included in this compilation, details are included in the endnotes.
For more information about any editorial changes made in this compilation, see the endnotes.

If the compiled law is modified by another law, the compiled law operates as modified but the modification does not amend the text of the law. Accordingly, this compilation does not show the text of the compiled law as modified. For more information on any modifications, see the series page on the Legislation Register for the compiled law.
If a provision of the compiled law has been repealed in accordance with a provision of the law, details are included in the endnotes.

section.heading: Applications for renewal of spectrum licences

content.p: A licensee of a spectrum licence may apply to the ACMA for the licence to be renewed.
If there is a renewal application period for the licence, the application must be made within the renewal application period.
If there is no renewal application period for the licence, the application must be made within the 2-year period ending when the licence is due to expire.
The application must:
be made in a manner approved, in writing, by the ACMA; and
be in a form approved, in writing, by the ACMA; and
be accompanied by such information (if any) as is specified in an instrument under subsection (6); and
be accompanied by such documents (if any) as are specified in an instrument under subsection (7).
The ACMA may approve different forms for different applications.
The ACMA may, by legislative instrument, specify information for the purposes of paragraph (4)(c).
The ACMA may, by legislative instrument, specify documents for the purposes of paragraph (4)(d).
An instrument under paragraph (4)(a) is a notifiable instrument.
An approved form of application may provide for verification by statutory declaration of statements in applications.
Deemed applications
If:
the ACMA gives a person a notice that is expressed to be a licence renewal notice; and
the notice relates to one or more spectrum licences held by the person; and
in response to the notice, the person:
pays to the ACMA (on behalf of the Commonwealth) the amount specified in the notice as the amount due; and
does so on or before the day specified in the notice as the payment due date;
then:
if the notice relates to a single spectrum licence—the person is taken to have made an application under subsection (1) for the licence to be renewed; and
if the notice relates to 2 or more spectrum licences—the person is taken to have made separate applications under subsection (1) for each of those licences to be renewed; and
subsection (4) does not apply to that application or those applications, as the case requires.

If an application is made for the renewal of a spectrum licence, the ACMA may, by written notice given to the applicant, require the applicant to give the ACMA, within the period specified in the notice, further information in connection with the application.
If the applicant breaches the requirement, the ACMA may, by written notice given to the applicant:
refuse to consider the application; or
refuse to take any action, or any further action, in relation to the application.

When an application is made for the renewal of a spectrum licence, the ACMA may, without following the procedures determined under section 60, renew the licence by issuing to the applicant a new spectrum licence.
Subsection (1) does not imply that the ACMA must renew the licence without the applicant:
paying to the ACMA the spectrum access charge for issuing the new spectrum licence; or
reaching an agreement with the ACMA for payment of that spectrum access charge.
The ACMA must not renew the licence if the licence included a renewal statement to the effect that the licence cannot be renewed.

If the licence included a renewal statement to the effect that the licence may be renewed at the discretion of the ACMA so long as specified circumstances exist, the ACMA must not renew the licence unless the ACMA is satisfied that the specified circumstances exist.

The ACMA must not renew the licence by issuing a new spectrum licence that specifies a period for the purposes of subsection 65(2) that is 10 years or longer unless the ACMA is satisfied that it is in the public interest to do so.
If the licence included a public interest statement, the ACMA must not renew the licence unless the ACMA is satisfied that it is in the public interest to do so.
In deciding whether to renew the licence, the ACMA must have regard to:
all matters that it considers relevant; and
without limiting paragraph (a), the effect on radiocommunications of the proposed operation of the radiocommunications devices that would be authorised under the new spectrum licence.
In deciding whether to renew the licence, the ACMA may have regard to the following matters:
whether the applicant has an outstanding liability to pay an amount of:
apparatus licence tax; or
spectrum licence tax; or
spectrum access charge; or
interim tax;
whether the applicant has contravened a condition of the licence;
whether the following conditions are satisfied:
a person authorised by the applicant under section 68 in relation to the licence has contravened a condition of the licence;
the applicant was aware, or ought reasonably to have been aware, of the contravention;
the applicant failed to take reasonable steps to prevent the contravention;
whether the applicant held another licence that was cancelled during the previous 2 years (otherwise than under section 87, 128B, 153H or 307).
The new spectrum licence comes into force, or is taken to have come into force, immediately after the expiration of the licence that it replaces.
The conditions of the new spectrum licence need not be the same as those of the licence that it replaces.

ensuring that designated radiocommunications receivers are not supplied to persons intending to operate those receivers unless those persons are authorised by or under this Act to operate those receivers;
an objective specified in the legislative rules;
an objective that is incidental or ancillary to any of the above objectives.
Before making equipment rules directed towards achieving the objective mentioned in paragraph (3)(e), the ACMA must consult ARPANSA (the Australian Radiation Protection and Nuclear Safety Agency).
The equipment rules may only be made to the extent that they are supported by one or more of the following provisions of the Constitution:
paragraph 51(i);
paragraph 51(v);
paragraph 51(vi);
paragraph 51(vii);
paragraph 51(viii);
paragraph 51(xiii);
paragraph 51(xiv);
paragraph 51(xv);
paragraph 51(xx);
paragraph 51(xxix);
paragraph 51(xxxix);
section 52;
section 122.
The equipment rules may prescribe standards for equipment.
Standards may require equipment:
to have particular design features; or
to meet particular performance requirements.
(3) A standard may be of general application or may be limited as provided in the equipment rules. This subsection does not limit subsection 33(3A) of the Acts Interpretation Act 1901.
This section does not, by implication, limit subsection 156(1).
This section has effect subject to subsection 156(3).
Obligations and prohibitions
The equipment rules may impose obligations or prohibitions in relation to equipment.
The equipment rules may impose obligations:
to ensure that quality assurance programs in relation to equipment are conducted; or
to ensure that tests in relation to equipment are conducted; or
to ensure that labels are applied to equipment; or
to ensure that records are kept or retained; or
to ensure that a thing specified in the legislative rules is done.
The equipment rules may impose obligations or prohibitions that relate to:
the operation of equipment; or
the supply of equipment; or
offers to supply equipment; or
the possession of equipment; or
the import of equipment.
If the equipment rules impose an obligation on a person to cause a thing to be done, the rules may require that the thing be done by another specified person.
Note: For specification by class, see subsection 13(3) of the Legislation Act 2003.

If the equipment rules impose an obligation on a person to cause a thing to be done, the equipment rules may require that the thing be done by another person holding an accreditation of a specified kind.
If the equipment rules impose an obligation on a person to cause a thing to be done, the equipment rules may require that the thing be done by another person who:
satisfies the conditions specified in the equipment rules; and
is approved, in writing, by a person holding an accreditation of a specified kind.

If the equipment rules impose an obligation on a person to cause a thing to be done, the equipment rules may require that the thing be done by another person who is approved, in writing, by a person holding an accreditation of a specified kind.
The equipment rules may prohibit a person from:
supplying; or
offering to supply;
a specified kind of equipment unless the person satisfies one or more specified conditions.
The equipment rules may require that, if:
the supply of equipment to a person; or
an offer to supply equipment to a person;
involves the person accessing the supplier’s website, the supplier must ensure that, before the equipment is supplied to the person, the person’s attention is drawn to material that:
is on the website; and
complies with specified requirements.
The equipment rules may prohibit a person from applying a specified kind of label to equipment unless the person does so in specified circumstances.

The equipment rules may prohibit a person who supplies, or offers to supply, equipment from publishing a specified kind of material about the equipment on the person’s website unless the person does so in specified circumstances.
The equipment rules may prohibit a person from doing an act or thing specified in the legislative rules.
Permits
The equipment rules may prohibit the doing of an act or thing by a person unless:
the person holds a permit issued by the ACMA under the equipment rules; and
the permit authorises the person to do that act or thing.
An act or thing is not authorised by a permit if it is not in accordance with the conditions of the permit.
The equipment rules may make provision for:
the issue of permits by the ACMA; and
the inclusion by the ACMA of conditions in a permit; and
the cancellation of permits by the ACMA.
Note 1: Refusals to issue permits are reviewable under Part 5.6.
Note 2: Decisions about permit conditions are reviewable under Part 5.6.
Note 3: Cancellations of permits are reviewable under Part 5.6.
The equipment rules may make provision for ACMA to vary a permit by:
including one or more further conditions; or
varying any conditions of the permit; or
revoking any conditions of the permit.
Note: Decisions about permit conditions are reviewable under Part 5.6.
Other matters
Subsections (2) to (16) do not limit subsection (1).
Subsections (2) to (16) do not limit each other.
This section does not, by implication, limit subsection 156(1).
This section has effect subject to subsection 156(3).

section.heading: Breach of equipment rules and permit conditions

content.p: Offence
A person commits an offence if:
the person is subject to a prohibition imposed by the equipment rules; and
the prohibition does not consist of contravening a condition of a permit; and
the person engages in conduct; and
the person’s conduct contravenes the prohibition.
Penalty: 500 penalty units.
A person commits an offence if:
the person is subject to an obligation imposed by the equipment rules; and
the obligation is not an obligation to do an act or thing:
within a particular period; or
before a particular time; and
the obligation is not an obligation to keep or retain records; and
the obligation is not an obligation to comply with a condition of a permit; and
the person engages in conduct; and
the person’s conduct contravenes the obligation.
Penalty: 500 penalty units.
A person commits an offence if:
the person is subject to an obligation imposed by the equipment rules; and
the obligation is an obligation to do an act or thing:
within a particular period; or
before a particular time; and
the obligation is not an obligation to keep or retain records; and
the obligation is not an obligation to comply with a condition of a permit; and
the person engages in conduct; and
the person’s conduct contravenes the obligation.
Penalty: 500 penalty units.
The maximum penalty for each day that an offence against subsection (3) continues is 10% of the maximum penalty that could be imposed in respect of the principal offence.
Civil penalties
If:
a person is subject to a prohibition imposed by the equipment rules; and
the prohibition does not consist of contravening a condition of a permit;
the person must not contravene the prohibition.
Civil penalty: 500 penalty units.
If:
a person is subject to an obligation imposed by the equipment rules; and
the obligation is not an obligation to do an act or thing:
within a particular period; or
before a particular time; and
the obligation is not an obligation to keep or retain records; and
the obligation is not an obligation to comply with a condition of a permit;
the person must not contravene the obligation.
Civil penalty: 500 penalty units.
If:
a person is subject to an obligation imposed by the equipment rules; and
the obligation is an obligation to do an act or thing:
within a particular period; or
before a particular time; and
the obligation is not an obligation to keep or retain records; and
the obligation is not an obligation to comply with a condition of a permit;
the person must not contravene the obligation.
Civil penalty: 500 penalty units.
The maximum civil penalty for each day that a contravention of subsection (7) continues is 10% of the maximum civil penalty that can be imposed in respect of a contravention of that subsection.
Note: Subsection (7) is a continuing civil penalty provision under section 93 of the Regulatory Powers Act.
If:
a person is subject to an obligation imposed by the equipment rules; and
the obligation is an obligation to keep or retain records;
the person must not contravene the obligation.
Civil penalty: 30 penalty units.
If a person is the holder of a permit, the person must not contravene a condition of the permit.
Civil penalty: 100 penalty units.
Subsection (10) does not apply if the person has a reasonable excuse.
Note: A defendant bears an evidential burden in relation to the matter in this subsection (see section 96 of the Regulatory Powers Act).

section.heading: Equipment rules may confer powers on the ACMA

content.p: The equipment rules may make provision in relation to a matter by conferring a power on the ACMA.

section.heading: Equipment rules may confer powers on accredited persons

content.p: The equipment rules may make provision in relation to a matter by conferring a power on a person who holds a specified kind of accreditation.

The equipment rules may authorise a person who holds a specified kind of accreditation to charge fees in relation to the exercise by the person of a power conferred by the equipment rules. A fee must not be such as to amount to taxation.

section.heading: Equipment rules may authorise the charging of fees by certain persons

content.p: The equipment rules may authorise a person who is required, under rules made for the purposes of subsection 159(4) or (7), to do a thing, to charge fees in relation to the doing of the thing by the person. A fee must not be such as to amount to taxation.

section.heading: Divisions 4 and 5 do not limit the ACMA’s power to make equipment rules

content.p: Divisions 4 and 5 do not, by implication, limit the ACMA’s power to make equipment rules.

section.heading: Use or application of protected symbols

content.p: General prohibition
A person must not:
use in relation to a business, trade, profession or occupation; or
apply (as a trade mark or otherwise) to goods imported, manufactured, produced, sold, offered for sale or let on hire; or
use in relation to:
goods or services; or
the promotion (by any means) of the supply or use of goods or services;
a protected symbol, or a symbol so closely resembling a protected symbol as to be likely to be mistaken for it.
Civil penalty: 50 penalty units.
Nothing in subsection (1) limits anything else in that subsection.
Use or application—corporations power
A constitutional corporation must not:
use in relation to a business, trade, profession or occupation; or
apply (as a trade mark or otherwise) to goods imported, manufactured, produced, sold, offered for sale or let on hire; or
use in relation to:
goods or services; or
the promotion (by any means) of the supply or use of goods or services;
a protected symbol, or a symbol so closely resembling a protected symbol as to be likely to be mistaken for it.
Civil penalty: 50 penalty units.
Nothing in subsection (3) limits anything else in that subsection.
Use or application—other legislative powers
A person must not:
use in relation to a business, trade, profession or occupation; or
apply (as a trade mark or otherwise) to goods imported, manufactured, produced, sold, offered for sale or let on hire; or
use in relation to:
goods or services; or
the promotion (by any means) of the supply or use of goods or services;
a protected symbol, or a symbol so closely resembling a protected symbol as to be likely to be mistaken for it, if the use or application is in the course of, or in relation to:
trade or commerce between Australia and places outside Australia; or
trade or commerce among the States; or
trade or commerce within a Territory, between a State and a Territory or between 2 Territories; or
the supply of goods or services to:
the Commonwealth; or
a Territory; or
an authority or instrumentality of the Commonwealth; or
an authority or instrumentality of a Territory; or
the defence of Australia; or
the operation of lighthouses, lightships, beacons or buoys; or
astronomical or meteorological observations; or
an activity of a constitutional corporation; or
banking, other than State banking; or
insurance, other than State insurance; or
weighing or measuring.
Civil penalty: 50 penalty units.
Nothing in subsection (5) limits anything else in that subsection.
Exceptions
Subsections (1), (3) and (5) do not apply to a person who uses or applies a protected symbol for the purposes of:
labelling equipment in accordance with the equipment rules; or
(b) labelling customer equipment (within the meaning of the Telecommunications Act 1997) or customer cabling (within the meaning of that Act), in accordance with section 407 of that Act.
Subsections (1), (3) and (5) do not apply to a person who uses or applies a protected symbol for a purpose of a kind specified in a determination under subsection (9).
The ACMA may, by legislative instrument, determine one or more specified kinds of purpose for the purposes of subsection (8).
The equipment rules may provide that subsections (1), (3) and (5) do not apply in relation to a specified use or application of a protected symbol.
(1) For the purposes of this Act, protected symbol means a symbol:
the design of which is set out in a determination under subsection (2); and
a purpose of which, after the commencement of this section, is to indicate compliance by equipment with any standards that:
are prescribed by the equipment rules; and
are applicable to the equipment.
The ACMA may, by legislative instrument, determine one or more designs for the purposes of paragraph (1)(a).
Labels applied to equipment
For the purposes of this Act, if:
a label is applied to equipment; and
the label embodies a symbol referred to in subsection (1);
the label is taken to indicate that the equipment meets the requirements of any standards that:
are prescribed by the equipment rules; and
are applicable to the equipment.
Subdivision A—Interim bans
(1) The ACMA may, by notifiable instrument, impose an interim ban on equipment of a specified kind if:
(a) the ACMA has reasonable grounds to believe that equipment of that kind is designed to have an adverse effect on radiocommunications; or
(b) the ACMA has reasonable grounds to believe that a reasonably foreseeable use (including a misuse) of equipment of that kind would be likely to substantially:
interfere with radiocommunications; or
disrupt or disturb radiocommunications in any other way; or
both:
equipment of that kind consists of radiocommunications transmitters; and
the ACMA has reasonable grounds to believe that radio emissions resulting from the operation of equipment of that kind would be likely to adversely affect the health or safety of individuals.
Publication
If the ACMA makes a notifiable instrument imposing an interim ban, the ACMA must publish a notice that sets out:
a statement to the effect that the ban has been imposed; and
the time when the ban came, or is to come, into force; and
the kind of equipment to which the ban relates; and
the reason or reasons for imposing the ban.
The following provisions have effect:
the ACMA must publish a notice under subsection (2) on the ACMA’s website;
the legislative rules may provide that the ACMA must also publish a notice under subsection (2) in accordance with the legislative rules.
An interim ban imposed by the ACMA:
comes into force on the day specified in the instrument imposing the ban; and
subject to this Act, remains in force for 60 days.
If an interim ban is in force, the ACMA may, by notifiable instrument, extend the period for which the ban is in force by a period of up to 30 days.
If an interim ban is in force:
the ACMA may, by notifiable instrument, revoke the ban; and
the revocation takes effect on the day specified in the instrument.
If:
an interim ban on equipment of a particular kind is in force; and
a permanent ban on equipment of that kind comes into force;
the interim ban is revoked when the permanent ban comes into force.
Supply
A person must not supply equipment of a particular kind to another person if:
the other person intends to operate the equipment; and
an interim ban on equipment of that kind is in force.
Civil penalty: 200 penalty units.
Offer to supply
A person must not offer to supply equipment of a particular kind to another person if:
the other person intends to operate the equipment; and
an interim ban on equipment of that kind is in force.
Civil penalty: 200 penalty units.
Operation
A person must not operate equipment of a particular kind if an interim ban on equipment of that kind is in force.
Civil penalty: 200 penalty units.
If:
a person contravenes subsection (1), (2) or (3); and
another person suffers loss or damage because of a reasonably foreseeable use (including a misuse) of the equipment;
the other person is taken, for the purposes of this Division, to have suffered the loss or damage because of the contravention.
If:
(a) a person (the claimant) suffers loss or damage because of conduct engaged in by another person; and
the conduct contravened subsection 170(1), (2) or (3);
the claimant may recover the amount of the loss or damage by action in the Federal Court or the Federal Circuit Court of Australia against:
that other person; or
any person involved in the contravention.
An action under subsection (1) may be commenced at any time within 6 years after the day on which the cause of action that relates to the conduct accrued.
A reference in this section to a person involved in the contravention is a reference to a person who has:
aided, abetted, counselled or procured the contravention; or
induced the contravention, whether through threats or promises or otherwise; or
been in any way (directly or indirectly) knowingly concerned in or a party to the contravention; or
conspired with others to effect the contravention.
Subdivision B—Permanent bans
(1) The ACMA may, by legislative instrument, impose a permanent ban on equipment of a specified kind if:
the ACMA is satisfied that equipment of that kind is designed to have an adverse effect on radiocommunications; or
the ACMA is satisfied that a reasonably foreseeable use (including a misuse) of equipment of that kind would be likely to substantially:
interfere with radiocommunications; or
disrupt or disturb radiocommunications in any other way; or
both:
equipment of that kind consists of radiocommunications transmitters; and
the ACMA is satisfied that radio emissions resulting from the operation of equipment of that kind would be likely to adversely affect the health or safety of individuals.
Before imposing a permanent ban on the grounds mentioned in paragraph (1)(c), the ACMA must consult ARPANSA (the Australian Radiation Protection and Nuclear Safety Agency).
Publication
If the ACMA makes a legislative instrument imposing a permanent ban, the ACMA must publish a notice that sets out:
a statement to the effect that the ban has been imposed; and
the time when the ban came, or is to come, into force; and
the kind of equipment to which the ban relates; and
the reason or reasons for imposing the ban.
The following provisions have effect:
the ACMA must publish a notice under subsection (3) on the ACMA’s website;
the legislative rules may provide that the ACMA must also publish a notice under subsection (3) in accordance with the legislative rules.

section.heading: When permanent bans come into force

content.p: A permanent ban comes into force on the day specified by the ACMA in the instrument imposing the ban.
If a permanent ban is in force:
the ACMA may, by legislative instrument, revoke the ban; and
the revocation takes effect on the day specified in the instrument.
Supply
A person commits an offence if:
the person supplies equipment of a particular kind to another person who intends to operate the equipment; and
a permanent ban on equipment of that kind is in force.
Penalty: Imprisonment for 2 years or 1,000 penalty units, or both.
Offer to supply
A person commits an offence if:
the person offers to supply equipment of a particular kind to another person who intends to operate the equipment; and
a permanent ban on equipment of that kind is in force.
Penalty: Imprisonment for 2 years or 1,000 penalty units, or both.
Operation
A person commits an offence if:
the person operates equipment of a particular kind; and
a permanent ban on equipment of that kind is in force.
Penalty: Imprisonment for 2 years or 1,000 penalty units, or both.
Possession
A person commits an offence if:
the person has equipment of a particular kind in the person’s possession; and
the possession is for the purpose of:
operating the equipment; or
supplying the equipment to another person who intends to operate the equipment; and
a permanent ban on equipment of that kind is in force.
Penalty for contravention of this subsection: Imprisonment for 2 years or 1,000 penalty units, or both.
Supply
A person must not supply equipment of a particular kind to another person if:
the other person intends to operate the equipment; and
a permanent ban on equipment of that kind is in force.
Civil penalty: 1,000 penalty units.
Offer to supply
A person must not offer to supply equipment of a particular kind to another person if:
the other person intends to operate the equipment; and
a permanent ban on equipment of that kind is in force.
Civil penalty: 1,000 penalty units.
Operation
A person must not operate equipment of a particular kind if a permanent ban on equipment of that kind is in force.
Civil penalty: 1,000 penalty units.
Possession
A person must not have equipment of a particular kind in the person’s possession if:
a permanent ban on equipment of that kind is in force; and
the possession is for the purpose of:
operating the equipment; or
supplying the equipment to another person who intends to operate the equipment.
Civil penalty: 1,000 penalty units.
If:
a person contravenes subsection (1), (2), (3) or (4); and
another person suffers loss or damage because of a reasonably foreseeable use (including a misuse) of the equipment;
the other person is taken, for the purposes of this Division, to have suffered the loss or damage because of the contravention.
If:
(a) a person (the claimant) suffers loss or damage because of conduct engaged in by another person; and
the conduct contravened subsection 176(1), (2), (3) or (4);
the claimant may recover the amount of the loss or damage by action in the Federal Court or the Federal Circuit Court of Australia against:
that other person; or
any person involved in the contravention.
An action under subsection (1) may be commenced at any time within 6 years after the day on which the cause of action that relates to the conduct accrued.
A reference in this section to a person involved in the contravention is a reference to a person who has:
aided, abetted, counselled or procured the contravention; or
induced the contravention, whether through threats or promises or otherwise; or
been in any way (directly or indirectly) knowingly concerned in or a party to the contravention; or
conspired with others to effect the contravention.
Subdivision C—Presumptions
Presumption relating to supply or offer to supply
For the purposes of subsections 170(1) and (2), 175(1) and (2) and 176(1) and (2), if:
(a) at a particular time, a person (the first person) supplies, or offers to supply, equipment to another person; and
the equipment can be operated;

it must be presumed that the other person intends to operate the equipment, unless the first person adduces or points to evidence that suggests a reasonable possibility that, at that time, the other person did not intend to operate the equipment.
Presumptions relating to possession
For the purposes of subsections 175(4) and 176(4), if:
at a particular time, a person has equipment in the person’s possession, otherwise than for the purpose of supplying the equipment to another person; and
the equipment can be operated;

it must be presumed that the person has the equipment in the person’s possession for the purpose of operating the equipment, unless the person adduces or points to evidence that suggests a reasonable possibility that, at that time, the person did not have the equipment in the person’s possession for the purpose of operating the equipment.
For the purposes of subsections 175(4) and 176(4), if:
(a) at a particular time, a person (the first person) has equipment in the person’s possession for the purpose of supplying the equipment to another person; and
the equipment can be operated;

it must be presumed that the other person intends to operate the equipment, unless the first person adduces or points to evidence that suggests a reasonable possibility that, at that time, the other person did not intend to operate the equipment.
When equipment can be operated
For the purposes of paragraphs (1)(b), (2)(b) and (3)(b), it is immaterial whether the equipment can be operated:
immediately; or
after taking one or more steps (for example, the connection of the equipment to a power supply).
Subdivision D—Amnesty for banned equipment
Amnesty period
The ACMA may, by notifiable instrument, declare that, for the purposes of subsection (2), a specified period is an amnesty period for a specified permanent ban.
Amnesty
If:
a permanent ban on equipment of a particular kind is in force; and
an amnesty period has been declared under subsection (1) for the ban;
then:
the owner of equipment of that kind may, during the amnesty period for the ban, agree with the ACMA (on behalf of the Commonwealth) to forfeit the equipment to the Commonwealth; and
if the owner does so—subsections 175(4) and 176(4), to the extent to which they relate to the ban, do not apply, and are taken never to have applied, to the possession of the equipment by:
the owner; or
any other person.

section.heading: The ACMA may take possession of equipment

content.p: If the owner of equipment agrees, in accordance with section 179, to forfeit the equipment to the Commonwealth:
the ACMA may take possession of the equipment; and
if the ACMA does so—the ACMA must give the owner a receipt for the equipment taken into possession.
If:
the ACMA has purported to take possession of equipment under subsection (1); and
the ACMA was not entitled to take possession of the equipment under that subsection;
the ACMA must take all reasonable steps to return the equipment to the owner of the equipment.

section.heading: Forfeiture of equipment to the Commonwealth

content.p: If:
the ACMA has taken possession of equipment under subsection 180(1); and
at least 90 days have passed since the ACMA gave the owner a receipt under paragraph 180(1)(b) for the equipment;
the ACMA may declare, in writing, that the equipment is forfeited to the Commonwealth.
The ACMA must give a copy of the declaration to the owner of the equipment.
Deemed forfeiture
If:
the owner of equipment agrees, in accordance with section 179, to forfeit the equipment to the Commonwealth; and
the ACMA has taken possession of the equipment under subsection 180(1); and

the ACMA has not, within the 120-day period beginning at the start of the day when the ACMA gave the owner a receipt under paragraph 180(1)(b) for the equipment, made a declaration under subsection (1) of this section that the equipment is forfeited to the Commonwealth;
then, at the end of the 120-day period, the equipment is forfeited to the Commonwealth.

section.heading: Forfeited equipment may be sold, destroyed or otherwise disposed of

content.p: Equipment forfeited under section 181:
may be sold, destroyed or otherwise disposed of in accordance with the directions of the ACMA; and
pending such directions, must be kept in such custody as the ACMA directs.
Subdivision A—Compulsory recall of equipment
Equipment that will or may cause substantial disruption, substantial disturbance or substantial interference to radiocommunications
(1) The ACMA may, by legislative instrument, issue a recall notice for equipment of a specified kind if:
a person, in trade or commerce, supplies, or has supplied, equipment of that kind; and

the ACMA is satisfied that a reasonably foreseeable use (including a misuse) of such equipment will or may cause substantial disruption, substantial disturbance or substantial interference to radiocommunications; and

the ACMA is satisfied that one or more suppliers of such equipment have not taken satisfactory action to prevent that equipment causing substantial disruption, substantial disturbance or substantial interference to radiocommunications.
Equipment designed to have an adverse effect on radiocommunications
(2) The ACMA may, by legislative instrument, issue a recall notice for equipment of a specified kind if:
a person, in trade or commerce, supplies, or has supplied, equipment of that kind; and
the ACMA is satisfied that equipment of that kind is designed to have an adverse effect on radiocommunications.
Equipment likely to adversely affect health or safety
(3) The ACMA may, by legislative instrument, issue a recall notice for equipment of a specified kind if:
equipment of that kind consists of radiocommunications transmitters; and
a person, in trade or commerce, supplies, or has supplied, equipment of that kind; and
the ACMA is satisfied that radio emissions resulting from the operation of equipment of that kind would be likely to adversely affect the health or safety of individuals.
Permanent ban
(4) The ACMA may, by legislative instrument, issue a recall notice for equipment of a specified kind if:
a person, in trade or commerce, supplies, or has supplied, equipment of that kind; and
a permanent ban on such equipment is in force; and
the ACMA is satisfied that one or more suppliers of such equipment have not taken satisfactory action to recall such equipment so supplied by those suppliers.
Publication
If the ACMA, by legislative instrument, issues a recall notice under subsection (1), (2), (3) or (4), the ACMA must publish a notice that sets out:
a statement to the effect that the recall notice has been issued; and
the time when the recall notice commences, or is to commence; and
the kind of equipment to which the recall notice relates; and
the reason or reasons for issuing the recall notice.
The following provisions have effect:
the ACMA must publish a notice under subsection (5) on the ACMA’s website;
the legislative rules may provide that the ACMA must also publish a notice under subsection (5) in accordance with the legislative rules.
Other matters
It is not necessary, for the purposes of paragraph (1)(a) or (c), (2)(a), (3)(b) or (4)(a) or (c), for the ACMA to know the identities of any of the suppliers of the equipment.
A recall notice for equipment may be issued under subsection (1), (2), (3) or (4) even if the equipment has become fixtures since the time the equipment was supplied.
A recall notice for equipment may require one or more suppliers of the equipment to take one or more of the following actions:
recall the equipment;
disclose to the public, or to a class of persons specified in the notice, the reasons for the issue of the recall notice;
inform the public, or a class of persons specified in the notice, that the supplier undertakes to do whichever of the following the supplier thinks is appropriate:
repair or modify the equipment;
replace the equipment;
refund to a person to whom the equipment was supplied (whether by the supplier or by another person), and who returns the equipment, the price paid for the equipment;
if an undertaking is given by a supplier in accordance with paragraph (c):
comply with the undertaking; and
comply with section 185 in relation to the undertaking;
disclose to the public, or to a class of persons specified in the notice, procedures as specified in the notice for disposing of the equipment.
The recall notice may specify:
the manner in which the action required to be taken by the notice must be taken; and
the period within which the action must be taken.
If the recall notice requires a supplier of the equipment to take action of a kind referred to in paragraph (1)(c), the ACMA may specify in the notice that, if:
the supplier undertakes to refund the price paid for equipment; and
a period of more than 12 months has elapsed since a person (whether or not the person to whom the refund is to be made) acquired the equipment from the supplier;
the amount of a refund may be reduced by the supplier by an amount, calculated in a manner specified in the notice, that is attributable to the use which a person has had of the equipment.

section.heading: Obligations of a supplier in relation to a recall notice

content.p: Scope
This section applies if a recall notice for equipment requires a supplier to take action of a kind referred to in paragraph 184(1)(c).
Obligations—repair or modify
If:
the recall notice was issued under subsection 183(1); and
the supplier undertakes to repair or modify the equipment;
the supplier must cause the equipment to be repaired or modified so that:
a reasonably foreseeable use or misuse of the equipment will not cause substantial disruption, substantial disturbance or substantial interference to radiocommunications; and
the equipment is not covered by an interim ban, or a permanent ban, that is in force.
If:
the recall notice was issued under subsection 183(2); and
the supplier undertakes to repair or modify the equipment;
the supplier must cause the equipment to be repaired or modified so that:
the equipment would not be likely to have an adverse effect on radiocommunications; and
the equipment is not covered by an interim ban, or a permanent ban, that is in force.
If:
the recall notice was issued under subsection 183(3); and

If:
the recall notice was issued under subsection 183(1); and
the supplier undertakes to replace the equipment;
the supplier must replace the equipment with similar equipment that satisfies the following conditions:
a reasonably foreseeable use or misuse of the similar equipment will not cause substantial disruption, substantial disturbance or substantial interference to radiocommunications;
the similar equipment is not covered by an interim ban, or a permanent ban, that is in force.
If:
the recall notice was issued under subsection 183(2); and
the supplier undertakes to replace the equipment;
the supplier must replace the equipment with similar equipment that satisfies the following conditions:
the similar equipment would not be likely to have an adverse effect on radiocommunications;
the similar equipment is not covered by an interim ban, or a permanent ban, that is in force.
If:
the recall notice was issued under subsection 183(3); and
the supplier undertakes to replace the equipment;
the supplier must replace the equipment with similar equipment that satisfies the following conditions:
radio emissions resulting from a reasonably foreseeable use (including a misuse) of the similar equipment would not be likely to adversely affect the health or safety of individuals;
the similar equipment is not covered by an interim ban, or a permanent ban, that is in force.

to repair or modify the equipment; or
to replace the equipment;

A person commits an offence if:
a recall notice for equipment is in force; and
the notice requires the person to do one or more things; and
the person engages in conduct; and
the person’s conduct contravenes the notice.

If:
a recall notice for equipment is in force; and
the notice requires a person to do one or more things;
the person must comply with the notice.

If:

section.heading: When a forfeiture notice may be given

content.p: If a designated forfeiture officer believes on reasonable grounds that:
a person has contravened a provision subject to a forfeiture notice under this Division; and
a thing was used, or otherwise involved, in the contravention of the provision;
the designated forfeiture officer may give to the person a forfeiture notice for the alleged contravention.
The forfeiture notice must be expressed to relate to the thing.
The forfeiture notice must be given within 12 months after the day on which the contravention is alleged to have taken place.
A designated forfeiture officer may give a person a single forfeiture notice relating to multiple alleged contraventions (whether of the same provision or different provisions).
A person must not be given:
a forfeiture notice; and
an infringement notice under Part 5 of the Regulatory Powers Act;
that relate to the same alleged contravention.

section.heading: Matters to be included in a forfeiture notice

content.p: A forfeiture notice must:
be identified by a unique number; and
state the day on which the notice is given; and
state the name of the person to whom the notice is given; and
state:
the name and contact details of the person who gave the notice; and
that the person is a designated forfeiture officer; and
give brief details of the alleged contravention or contraventions to which the notice relates, including:
the provision or the provisions that were allegedly contravened; and
the maximum penalty that a court could impose for each contravention, if the provision or those provisions were contravened; and
the time (if known) and day of, and the place of, each alleged contravention; and
describe the thing to which the notice relates; and

(g) state that, if, within 28 days after the day the notice is given, the owner of the thing agrees with the ACMA (on behalf of the Commonwealth) to forfeit the thing to the Commonwealth, then (unless the notice is withdrawn) proceedings seeking a civil penalty order or orders will not be brought in relation to the alleged contravention or contraventions; and
state that agreeing to forfeit the thing to the Commonwealth is not an admission of guilt or liability; and
state that the person to whom the notice is given may apply to the ACMA to have the period specified in the notice extended; and

state that the owner of the thing may choose not to agree to forfeit the thing to the Commonwealth and, if the owner so chooses, proceedings seeking a civil penalty order or orders may be brought in relation to the alleged contravention or contraventions; and
set out how the notice can be withdrawn; and
state that if the notice is withdrawn, proceedings seeking a civil penalty order or orders may be brought in relation to the alleged contravention or contraventions; and
state that the person to whom the notice is given may make written representations to the ACMA seeking the withdrawal of the notice.
To avoid doubt, the person to whom a forfeiture notice is given may be the owner of the thing to which the notice relates.
If:
a forfeiture notice relating to a thing is given to a person; and
the owner of the thing agrees, in accordance with the notice, to forfeit the thing to the Commonwealth;
the owner is not entitled to revoke the agreement.

section.heading: Extension of time to agree to forfeit a thing to the Commonwealth

content.p: A person to whom a forfeiture notice has been given may apply to the ACMA for an extension of the period referred to in paragraph 275(1)(g).
If the application is made before the end of that period, the ACMA may, in writing, extend that period. The ACMA may do so before or after the end of that period.

If the ACMA extends that period, a reference in this Division, or in a notice or other instrument under this Division, to the period referred to in paragraph 275(1)(g) is taken to be a reference to that period so extended.

If the ACMA does not extend that period, a reference in this Division, or in a notice or other instrument under this Division, to the period referred to in paragraph 275(1)(g) is taken to be a reference to the period that ends on the later of the following days:
the day that is the last day of the period referred to in paragraph 275(1)(g);
the day that is 7 days after the day the person was given notice of the ACMA’s decision not to extend.
The ACMA may extend that period more than once under subsection (2).

A person to whom a forfeiture notice has been given may make written representations to the ACMA seeking the withdrawal of the notice.
Withdrawal of notice
The ACMA may withdraw a forfeiture notice given to a person, so long as the thing to which the notice relates has not been forfeited to the Commonwealth.
